name: Ivan Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior back-end developer at Routewise, a company that makes route-planning software for delivery vans. My day starts with stand-up at half nine, then I work on the bit of the system that tells a driver which street to do next. I have an AI assistant open the whole time, and I use it for everything from first drafts of code to explaining error messages I don't understand. I'm honestly not the strongest coder on the team, but I'm quick, and I like that.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part you enjoy most, and the part that wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the days when a driver's route gets ten minutes shorter because of something I changed. What wears me out is the on-call week once a month, when my phone can buzz at three in the morning because a depot's map broke. I share a flat with my friend Kofi, who's a sound engineer, so at least someone else is usually awake at three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. I'd be a bit disappointed, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so to the hype people, but also that the tools are still really useful day to day. Online I'd probably post something about how the real story was always about who owns the tools, not how clever they are. I'd keep pushing for a four-day week, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep my job and keep my edge, because I'm already fast with the tools. The downside is that I'm still a junior on junior pay in a city where rent keeps climbing. That problem was there before AI and it stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Routewise and ask for a pay review in March, using my ticket numbers as proof. I'd keep about four months of rent in savings and keep putting 200 a month into a cheap index fund. I'd also try to get off the on-call rota by offering to write better alerts with the AI assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit bored by the idea that nothing big happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use your ticket numbers as proof. Do you think you'd get the raise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small one. My manager Ruth likes speed, and I close a lot of tickets, but she also knows the seniors fix some of my code afterwards. I'd go in asking for eight percent and be happy with four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would still keep you up at night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the on-call week, really. My savings cover a few months and there are other software jobs in the city if Routewise went under. Rent going up again would annoy me, but it wouldn't scare me.

say: The tools are still **useful day to day**, even if the hype was overblown.
The real story was always **who owns the tools**, not how clever they are.
think: I keep my job and my **edge**, because I'm already fast with AI.
**Junior pay** against rising rent is a problem that stays either way.
do: Ask Ruth for a **pay review** in March using ticket numbers as proof.
Keep **four months** of rent saved and invest 200 a month.
Offer to write **better alerts** to get off the on-call rota.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **bored** by a future where nothing big happens.
S0.quote: I'd go in asking for eight percent and be happy with four.
fieldNote: He treats daily AI use as his **competitive edge** over stronger coders.
His only real stress is the **on-call week**, not job security.
Progressive views focus on **ownership and hours**, not on stopping the tools.

steps.text: Ask manager Ruth for an eight percent raise in March
Put 200 a month into a cheap index fund
Use the AI assistant to write better depot alerts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's closer to what I actually expect. Coding's on the list, obviously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at stand-up that the team should decide together how we use the tools, not have it handed down. Online I'd argue for companies paying into a retraining fund for every job they shrink. I'd also say juniors like me are the canaries here, and people should watch what happens to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine for a while, because I'm the one already using the tools all day. The people who'd struggle at Routewise are the testers and the two support staff who answer depot calls. The bit that worries me is that if AI writes most code, the company won't need many people like me in five years either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to run a weekly session showing the team how I use the AI assistant, so I become the go-to person. I'd join the tech workers' union and suggest we ask for a no-layoffs promise tied to the new tools. I'd also start a small evening course in data engineering, because moving data around feels harder to automate than writing features.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a buzzy way. Like standing at the top of a slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the testers and support staff would struggle. Who in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta (a tester on my team) has been there eleven years, knows every depot by name and has never once opened an AI tool. I really like her, and I can already see the meeting where her role gets 'reviewed'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Routewise offered you a promotion to lead the AI rollout, but it meant cutting the testers, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to say no, and I think I'd ask for it without the cuts. If they said it's both or neither, I'd probably take it and fight for redeployment from the inside. I'm not proud of how fast I answered that.

say: Teams should decide **together** how AI tools are used, not have it handed down.
Companies should pay into a **retraining fund** for every job they shrink.
think: I'd be **fine for a while** because I already use the tools all day.
If AI writes most code, Routewise won't need **many juniors** in five years.
do: Run a **weekly session** showing the team how he uses the AI assistant.
Join the **tech union** and push for a no-layoffs promise.
Start an evening course in **data engineering**.
feel: **Uneasy** but excited, like standing at the top of a **slide**.

fieldNote: He openly admits he'd take a promotion that **cut testers**, then felt uneasy saying it.
His own job looks safe here, so the worry is for **colleagues like Marta**.
He mixes **union action** with personal positioning as the AI expert.

steps.text: Run weekly AI assistant sessions for the Routewise team
Join the tech union and push for a no-layoffs promise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. Okay, that's my whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that the gains have to be shared, through something like a basic income paid from AI profits. I'd be in every online thread about it, and I'd probably go to protests. At work I'd say what everyone's thinking: none of us are safe, including the seniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, being good with AI tools stops mattering when the AI doesn't need me to drive it. Everything I do is on a screen, so I'm in the first wave in 2028. The robots coming in 2031 only matter for my plan B, because hands-on work has three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop investing and keep every spare bit as cash, aiming for six months. I'd look for a hands-on side trade I could learn fast, maybe helping Kofi rig sound at gigs, because that's work in a room with people. In the first year after it lands I'd join whatever union or campaign is pushing for an AI dividend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops when I picture Ruth booking a short call with HR in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said sound rigging with Kofi. Is that a real plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half and half. Kofi already gets more gig work than he can take, and he's offered to teach me twice. It wouldn't pay my rent alone, but it's real money for three years while the robots catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum not to worry, which she would ignore. My dad drives a bus, so we'd have a strange conversation where his job outlasts my fancy one. He'd find that funnier than I would.

say: The gains must be shared, through a **basic income** paid from AI profits.
Nobody at Routewise is **safe**, including the seniors.
think: Being good with AI stops mattering when the **AI drives itself**.
Hands-on work has **three extra years**, which only helps a plan B.
do: Stop investing and hold **six months** of costs in cash.
Learn **sound rigging** from Kofi as a hands-on side trade.
Join the campaign for an **AI dividend** once it arrives.
feel: **Alarmed**, picturing Ruth booking a short call with **HR** in it.
S2.quote: My dad drives a bus, so we'd have a strange conversation where his job outlasts my fancy one.
fieldNote: His **AI skills** stop protecting him here, and he sees it right away.
He uses the **robot gap** to pick hands-on side work with a friend.
The bus-driver father shows how **status flips** under fast AGI.

steps.text: Hold six months of costs in cash, no investing
Learn sound rigging from Kofi and take gig shifts
Join the campaign for an AI dividend

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. It's still my whole job in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get a public retraining scheme running if politicians stop arguing. Online I'd be the guy posting the same chart every week, showing which jobs are shrinking. At work I'd push for the company to fund courses for everyone, not just the people they like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd ride it for three or four years, maybe even get promoted because I'm good with the tools. Then in 2031 it's over for desk work. The real question is what I'm doing in 2030, and I don't know yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep using the AI tools to get as much experience as possible. In the second year I'd start an evening course in electrical installation, because rigging and wiring use the same brain. I'd keep 200 a month going into savings, not shares, and keep the on-call money aside as my course fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious. There's a plan, so I'd mostly feel it on Sunday nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical installation and not something else hands-on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every robot and every server still needs someone to wire it, at least until 2034. I like fiddly logic, and wiring is logic you can touch. Kofi also says good electricians at venues are impossible to find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to make that plan work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the band, at least for a year or two. It's two evenings a week, and the course would need them. That one would hurt more than the money.

say: Five years is enough for a **public retraining** scheme if politicians stop arguing.
Routewise should fund **courses for everyone**, not just favourites.
think: I'd ride it **three or four years**, maybe even get promoted.
In **2031** desk work ends, and I don't know my 2030 plan yet.
do: Keep the job and gain as much **AI experience** as possible.
Start an evening course in **electrical installation** in year two.
Save **on-call pay** as a dedicated course fund.
feel: **Anxious** but busy, feeling it mostly on **Sunday nights**.
S3.quote: Every robot and every server still needs someone to wire it, at least until 2034.
fieldNote: He uses the three-year **robot gap** to justify electrical training.
Giving up the **band** hurts him more than any money cut.
Mood drops a notch from 2028 because he has a **plan and time**.

steps.text: Use AI tools daily to gain experience at Routewise
Start an evening electrical installation course in year two
Save on-call pay as a course fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can get it right, and anyone who wastes the decade should be held to account. I'd campaign for shorter weeks and public ownership of some of the big AI systems. I'd say it at work too, probably at the Christmas party, which nobody would thank me for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I can actually become a good developer first, then decide. I'd probably get to mid-level by 2029. I think I'd also be tempted to put off the hard choices, which is my weakness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in software for at least five years, using every new AI tool as it comes, and aim for a mid-level job by 2029. I'd keep investing 200 a month, because a decade gives shares time to grow. Around 2031 I'd start electrical training so I'm qualified before the robots in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. I'd feel like I have time to be young for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be tempted to put off hard choices. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing a date down. I'd put 'start electrician course' in my calendar for September 2031 and tell my flatmate Kofi so he nags me. I know myself well enough to need that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything about where you live or who with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If I'm still earning a developer wage for five more years, I might move out of the shared flat into my own place. I'd want to stay near Kofi though, because the side work would come through him.

Some big AI systems should be under **public ownership**.

My weakness is **putting off** the hard choices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my whole edge disappears and I'd have no time to build the next one. What would help is a basic income or at least a year of paid retraining, with an electrician course I could actually get into. Waiting lists for those courses are already long.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who people would blame. I'd blame the owners and the politicians who let them keep everything, not the engineers. Being fast with the tools only matters while somebody still needs a person to hold them.

headlineQuote: Being fast with the tools only matters while somebody still needs a person to hold them.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old** junior back-end developer at Routewise, a route-planning software company.
He uses **AI tools all day** and treats speed as his edge over stronger coders.
His **progressive views** focus on who owns AI and who gets the gains.
He plans a **hands-on fallback** in sound rigging or electrical work, using the robot gap.
His mood moves from **calm** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** with AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his AI **edge** vanishes with no time to build another.

Real access to **electrician courses** without long waiting lists.
